title: The Rule of 72
body: Divide 72 by an annual return to get the years it takes money to double. At 12% a year, roughly six years; at 8%, nine. It is the fastest way to sanity-check any compounding or inflation claim in your head.

title: Opportunity cost
body: The real cost of any choice is the best alternative you gave up to make it. Cash sitting idle is not free; it is quietly losing the return it could have earned elsewhere. Every 'yes' is a hidden 'no' to something else.

title: The sunk cost fallacy
body: Money already spent should never justify spending more. 'We've come too far to quit' is how bad projects, bad investments and bad relationships get funded past the point of sense. Decide from where you are now, not from what you've buried.

title: Survivorship bias
body: In WWII, engineers wanted to armour the bullet holes on returning planes. Abraham Wald pointed out the opposite: armour where the survivors were NOT hit, because planes shot there never came back. You only see the winners, so the data lies.

title: The market for lemons
body: George Akerlof won a Nobel for a simple idea: when buyers can't tell good used cars from 'lemons', they only offer average prices, good sellers exit, and quality collapses. It explains insurance, hiring, and why trust is worth money.

title: Comparative advantage
body: Ricardo's counter-intuitive insight: two countries (or people) both gain from trade even if one is better at everything, as long as they specialise in what they're relatively best at. It's the strongest argument in all of economics.

title: Creative destruction
body: Schumpeter's engine of capitalism: growth comes from the new constantly destroying the old. The same force that builds Amazon guts the high street. Progress and disruption are not opposites; they are the same event seen from two sides.

title: Goodhart's Law
body: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' Reward call-centre staff for call volume and they hang up on you. Any metric you optimise hard enough eventually gets gamed. Watch what a KPI does to behaviour.

title: The Lindy effect
body: For ideas, books and technologies, life expectancy grows with age. Something that has survived 50 years will probably last another 50; this year's fad probably won't. The old is not outdated, it is battle-tested.

title: Margin of safety
body: Benjamin Graham's core rule: only buy an asset well below your estimate of its worth, so you're protected even when you're wrong. Bridges are built for ten times expected load. Invest the same way, because your estimate WILL be wrong.

title: Mr. Market
body: Graham imagined the market as a manic-depressive partner who shows up daily offering to buy or sell at wild prices. His moods are a service, not a signal: you're free to trade on his panic or ignore him. Price is what he says; value is your job.

title: Circle of competence
body: Buffett and Munger's discipline: know the boundary of what you actually understand, and stay inside it. The size of the circle matters far less than knowing exactly where its edge is. Most mistakes happen just outside it.

title: The economic moat
body: A durable competitive advantage that protects profits the way a moat protects a castle: brands (Coca-Cola), network effects (Visa), switching costs (SAP), or low-cost scale (Walmart). Without a moat, high returns invite competitors who compete them away.

title: Network effects
body: A product that gets more valuable as more people use it: one telephone is useless, a billion are indispensable. It creates winner-take-most markets and explains why WhatsApp, not its features, is why you can't leave WhatsApp.

title: The bullwhip effect
body: Small bumps in retail demand get amplified into wild swings up the supply chain, as each layer over-orders to be safe. A 5% blip at the shop becomes a factory boom-and-bust. It's why supply chains lurch between shortage and glut.

title: Jevons paradox
body: Making a resource more efficient can increase its total use, not reduce it. More fuel-efficient engines led to more driving, not less petrol. Efficiency lowers the cost of using something, and cheaper things get used more.

title: The Prisoner's Dilemma
body: Two suspects, each better off betraying the other, both end up worse than if they'd cooperated. It's the maths behind price wars, arms races and climate inaction: individually rational choices producing a collectively terrible outcome.

title: The tragedy of the commons
body: When a shared resource is free to all and owned by none, each user takes as much as they can and it collapses: overfished seas, jammed roads, polluted air. Shared costs plus private gains is a recipe for ruin unless someone sets rules.

title: Moral hazard
body: When you're shielded from the downside of your risks, you take more of them. Bail out a bank and it gambles again; insure a car fully and drivers get careless. Skin in the game keeps behaviour honest.

title: Loss aversion
body: Kahneman and Tversky found losing 1,000 rupees hurts about twice as much as gaining 1,000 feels good. It's why we hold losing stocks too long and sell winners too early, and why 'don't lose it' outsells 'you could win'.

title: Anchoring
body: The first number you hear drags your judgement toward it, even when it's random. A crossed-out 'was 9,999' price makes 4,999 feel cheap. Negotiators open high on purpose; the anchor does the work before you've thought.

title: The Dunning-Kruger effect
body: The less competent you are at something, the less equipped you are to notice, so beginners overrate themselves while experts, aware of the gaps, underrate themselves. Confidence and competence are not the same curve.

title: Regression to the mean
body: Extreme results tend to be followed by more average ones, for no deeper reason than luck evening out. Punish a pilot after a bad landing and the next is better; praise after a great one and it's worse. You can fool yourself into crediting the wrong cause.

title: The Pareto principle (80/20)
body: Roughly 80% of effects come from 20% of causes: a fifth of clients bring most revenue, a fifth of bugs cause most crashes. Find that vital 20% and you get most of the result for a fraction of the effort.

title: Parkinson's Law
body: 'Work expands to fill the time available for its completion.' Give a task a week and it takes a week; give it a day and it's often done. Tight deadlines aren't cruelty, they're a productivity tool.

title: Occam's razor
body: When explanations compete, prefer the one with the fewest assumptions. Not because simple is always true, but because it's the cheapest to test and the least likely to be a story you told yourself. Start simple, add complexity only when forced.

title: Hanlon's razor
body: 'Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity' or, more kindly, by carelessness and bad systems. Most of what looks like someone out to get you is just someone busy, tired, or unaware.

title: Chesterton's fence
body: Before you remove a rule or structure that seems pointless, first understand why it was put there. If you can't explain its purpose, you're not yet qualified to tear it down. Reformers who skip this step tend to recreate the original problem.

title: Second-order thinking
body: First-order: 'this raises prices, so cut them.' Second-order: 'and then a competitor matches, margins collapse, and we're worse off.' Ask 'and then what?' a few times. The best decisions look bad at the first level and good at the third.

title: The map is not the territory
body: Every model, spreadsheet and financial statement is a simplified map of a messier reality. Useful, but never the thing itself. Trouble starts when people manage the map, D/E ratios and NPS scores, and forget the territory it was meant to describe.

title: Antifragile
body: Taleb's word for things that don't just survive stress but improve from it: muscles under load, markets that clear crashes, careers that gain from small failures. The opposite of fragile isn't robust, it's something that wants a bit of disorder.

title: The black swan
body: Taleb's term for rare, high-impact events that look obvious only in hindsight: 2008, COVID, the fall of the USSR. We build models on the normal and get blindsided by the tails. Plan for the fact that the biggest events are the ones you didn't model.

title: Disruptive innovation
body: Clayton Christensen's insight: incumbents lose not by being lazy but by being rational. They chase their best customers upmarket while a cheaper, 'worse' entrant serves the ignored bottom, improves, and eats them from below. Steel mills, then Netflix.

title: Crossing the chasm
body: Geoffrey Moore's map of tech adoption: the hard gap is between early enthusiasts who tolerate rough products and the pragmatic majority who need proof and references. Many startups die in that chasm, mistaking early buzz for real demand.

title: Case study: Kodak
body: Kodak invented the digital camera in 1975, then buried it to protect its film profits. By the time digital was unstoppable, others owned it; Kodak filed for bankruptcy in 2012. The lesson: the thing that made you rich can be the thing you most need to cannibalise.

title: Case study: LTCM
body: Long-Term Capital Management had two Nobel laureates and models that said disaster was near-impossible. In 1998 the improbable happened, its huge leverage nearly took the financial system with it, and the Fed organised a bailout. Genius plus leverage is still leverage.

title: Case study: Enron
body: Enron used 'mark-to-market' accounting to book years of imagined future profit today, and off-balance-sheet vehicles to hide debt. It was America's most admired company right up to its 2001 collapse. When you can't understand how a firm makes money, that's the finding.

title: Case study: the PNB–Nirav Modi fraud
body: Jeweller Nirav Modi allegedly used fraudulent Letters of Undertaking from a single Punjab National Bank branch to raise around 14,000 crore rupees, undetected for years because the messaging system wasn't linked to the bank's core ledger. Controls only work if they're connected.

title: Tulip mania
body: In 1630s Holland, single tulip bulbs traded for the price of a house before collapsing to nothing. It's the original speculative bubble and a permanent reminder: 'this time is different' has been said before every crash, and it usually wasn't.

title: The efficient market hypothesis
body: The claim that asset prices already reflect all available information, so you can't reliably beat the market. Half of finance is built on it; the other half, including Buffett, is a standing argument against it. Both halves are worth understanding before you invest.

title: Veblen goods
body: Rare items where demand RISES as the price rises, because the high price IS the point: luxury watches, exclusive handbags. They break the normal demand curve. Sometimes you're not buying the thing, you're buying the fact that others can't.

title: Dollar-cost averaging
body: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals regardless of price. You buy more units when cheap and fewer when dear, which removes the impossible job of timing the market and the emotion that wrecks it. An Indian SIP is exactly this.

title: Via negativa
body: Improvement by subtraction: you often make things better faster by removing what's harmful than by adding what's good. Cut the bad client, the useless meeting, the junk food. What you avoid usually matters more than what you add.

title: The Overton window
body: The range of ideas the public currently considers acceptable to discuss. It shifts over time, and skilled actors move it deliberately by first floating 'unthinkable' positions. What's politically impossible one decade is common sense the next.
